All this place happened to be down in the basement, you know? It was down in the basement. I had a full show there. It was a good show. Casper Holstein, which was the proprietor, he was a very nice man. You didn't have to worry about your money. I mean, whether he did business or not, he always had a smile on his face. You see, if they wouldn't have many people all the week, he never tormented the band, say to the band, and, man, he's not playing. I mean, what's happening to the band, and what's this and what's that. Find all kind of excuses. On a Monday night, it was our pay night, and he'd come up to Emble Up and give Russell, give a little Russell Emble Up to pay us off, and with a big smile on his face. Never hear him complain. Never hear him complain. Never complain. He's a great man to work for. They kidnapped him one time. I don't know. Really? You see, yeah, yeah. He had a policy racket, you know, and they kidnapped him and kept him for about a couple of weeks. There was no way he was at. Look him find him. Detective looking all over for him. Had all the police force, I imagine, in New York looking for him, Casper Holstein. I think they gave the guys the money, though, and he didn't say anything. He saved his life. He never really said who he was. He knew the guys. So they had him someplace on it, some holes on it, some old building or something like that. So they treated him all right, but they wanted that ransom money. I forgot how much ransom money it was. I don't know if it was $2,000 or whatever. I can't recall. That's how it took a drag, huh? Maybe he was. That's Russell's arrangement, I know that. He's on Don, too. It's Russell's arrangement.
He did a lot of arrangements, you know.
Yeah.
Who else arranged for that band?
Around that time, uh... Bingham Addison? Well, Bingham Addison, you do.
Did you have many arrangers around, uh... saying King Oliver's times? Who else arranged for King Oliver other than... than Louis Russell? Or did Louis Russell arrange much for... For King Oliver?

No, well, uh... Oliver had his own ideas, I mean, what I think. I don't recall that Oliver had anything written down, I mean, it's... No, he's never writing nothing down. He never did write nothing down. I never seen no music up there. I don't remember, maybe he did, but I doubt it.
What about, uh... Louis Armstrong? Did he have any arrangers when you worked with him?

Well, yeah, he had, uh... Chapper Willett, and, well, a few others, I mean. Yeah. That Chapper Willett was one of the main arrangers. At the time I was with the big band there, wasn't out of college then.
What about Louis Russell?
Well, he's a pretty good arranger.
For Armstrong, too, he did some?
Well, he made a few introductions and things like that. I don't think he ever made a big arrangement, no. I can't recall. Nope.
Well that's funny. He would arrange for his own band, but not for Armstrong.
Well I think the office, I mean, had hired Chapper Willett to make all the arrangements. And Chapper and, it's another guy, I can't think.
What did the guy play?

No, he didn't play anything. He played the piano, I imagine, I mean, the arranger, I mean. I never heard him play nothing. But I know he used to come to that arrangement. I don't know, I can't call the guy's name. I don't think you'll find him in there.
No, a colored guy, huh?
No, a white guy.
A white guy did the arrangements.

Yeah, he made, this number we played so fast, that music, swing that music, and all, and he arranged numbers like that. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Swing that music.
Wouldn't be anybody like Bob Haggard, the bass player with Bob Crosby.
I wouldn't bother, no, I wouldn't bother. Yeah.
Let me play a King Oliver thing for you now, another one.
What's your name, Rob?
Dead Man Blues. It's a Johnny Roll Morton tune. Vocalium 1057.
Yeah, that's the number. 1059?
1059? Yeah. Yeah, I see. Mm-hm.
Thank you. Sound like Don and Howard.

Sound like Don and Howard. Sound like Don and Howard. Sound like Don and Howard. Sound like Don and Howard. Sound like Don and Howard. They list Don and Howard, Stomp Evans, and Bonnie Begard. Yeah. So it might have been Don and Howard easily.
Yeah, that was Don and Howard. I know he's style of playing there. That's Don now.
It's Bud Scott and Bert Cobbs there. They sounded good there to me.
Yeah. Stomp Evans, Don and Bonnie Begard.
What was Stomp's name? Stomp or Stomp? Stomp.
He was a short guy?
Yeah, a little bit of a short guy. Where was he from?

I think he was from some part of Indiana if I am mistaken. Well, I think we better call it to a halt, don't you? Well, I don't know. I mean, it's up to you. Yeah, well, we've got visitors coming into town, you say? Oh, yeah. Well, those people come from Limestone, New York. That's right.
Yeah, yeah. Yeah. So we'll turn it off. Okay.

segments.title: Opening: location, date and Barbarin's full name
segments.summary: Recording setup at Tulane, the date, and how Barbarin got the names Adolph Paul, after his father's friend and his godfather, a music teacher.

segments.title: King Oliver record: Oliver's mute technique
segments.summary: A King Oliver record is played; Barbarin recalls the Brunswick/Vocalion issue, his own drumming and how Oliver worked his mute with his hand.

segments.title: Recording at the Plantation Cafe with Oliver; Stump Evans; Oliver's arranging
segments.summary: Barbarin recalls working at the Plantation when the record was made, identifies Stump Evans, remarks that Oliver was declining, and says Oliver gave ideas and dressed up stock tunes without arrangements.

segments.title: Someday Sweetheart and Oliver's ideas; Chicago players
segments.summary: Barbarin praises Oliver's ideas on Someday Sweetheart, then names a St. Louis trumpeter, Chicago musicians and Franz Jackson's band.

segments.chapter: Tuba players and New Orleans bands
segments.title: Early tuba players and New Orleans tuba men today
segments.summary: Hearing a tuba solo, Barbarin names Lawson Buford, Bill Moore and Boyd Cobb as great tuba men and discusses current New Orleans tuba players.

segments.chapter: Tuba players and New Orleans bands
segments.title: Funeral parade with Dave Bailey; Bailey's drumming and the union
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about a Sunday funeral where Barbarin's band met Bailey's; Barbarin praises Bailey and says the players should join the union.

segments.chapter: Tuba players and New Orleans bands
segments.title: Dave Bailey and Minor Hall in the Crescent City band; Chip
segments.summary: Barbarin recalls hearing Bailey and Minor Hall in a six-piece Crescent City band led by Chip, and learns Chip has died.

segments.chapter: Tuba players and New Orleans bands
segments.title: Where the bass players came from
segments.summary: Brief exchange on the origins of the tuba players Beaufort and Bill Moore.

segments.title: Barney Bigard's start on tenor and clarinet; Albert Nicholas in Oliver's band
segments.summary: Barbarin says Bigard began on tenor, took up clarinet at Tom Anderson's, and that Albert Nicholas was Oliver's featured clarinetist.

segments.title: Saxophone ideas, stock arrangements and recording in New York
segments.summary: Reed players took tone from popular 1920s sax bands, and stock arrangements were trimmed; Barbarin cannot recall one New York recording.

segments.title: Tuba records, Barbarin's age and Eddie Anderson
segments.summary: Lucille Higgins' recording, Barbarin joking about not telling his age, and a mention of Eddie Anderson.

segments.title: Wilton Crawley records and Larry Metcalf
segments.summary: Wilton Crawley's Victor records are played; Barbarin has never heard them, guesses the players and tries to find the record.

segments.title: Louis Russell record: Bobby Cheeks and Say the Word
segments.summary: Playing a Louis Russell Victor, Barbarin identifies trumpeter Bobby Cheeks, who has died.

segments.title: Going to Town: Henry Jones, Bingie Madison, Red Allen and Crawley
segments.summary: Barbarin identifies saxophonist Henry Jones and clarinetist Bingie Madison and debates Rex Stewart versus Red Allen on trumpet. He also names the clarinetist Crawley on Snake Up Dance.

segments.title: Wilton Crawley's stage act
segments.summary: Barbarin describes Crawley's comic act, singing, jokes and contortionist clarinet playing.

segments.title: Trumbauer, Eddie Lang and Bix
segments.summary: Barbarin liked Trumbauer's band, did not know Lang or Bix by name.

segments.title: Ease On Down and the Saratoga Club on Lenox Avenue
segments.summary: Barbarin says Ease On Down was a feature at the Saratoga Club, where he enjoyed the shows, and discusses Teddy Hill and Bob Williams.

segments.title: Saratoga Club and Casper Holstein as boss
segments.summary: Barbarin describes the basement club on Lenox Avenue and Holstein as a kind employer who paid on Mondays, and the story of his kidnapping.

segments.title: Arrangers for Russell, Oliver and Armstrong
segments.summary: Who arranged for Russell, Oliver and Armstrong: Oliver wrote nothing down, and Armstrong's office hired arrangers including a white man.

segments.title: Dead Man Blues: Darnell Howard, Stump Evans and Bonnie Bigard
segments.summary: Playing King Oliver's Dead Man Blues, they identify Darnell Howard, Stump Evans and Bigard and discuss the rhythm players.

segments.title: Closing the session
segments.summary: Barbarin suggests stopping because of visitors and the recorder is turned off.
